--- title: "Workbook suggested answers" --- ## Introduction {.unnumbered} This chapter presents the suggested `R` code to answer the workbook activities and exercises throughout the course labs in Quantitative Methods in the Social Sciences. This covers Lab 3 to Lab 10. Before looking at the answers, try asking your tutor for help. Also, we strongly recommend web resources, such as or . By solving the issues, you will learn a lot! ;) ## Lab 3. Data wrangling {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Load the packages library(tidyverse) library(haven) # Read the cleaned data from the .rds file cleaned_nilt <- readRDS("data/nilt_r_object.rds") # Read the original .sav file unclean_nilt <- read_sav("data/nilt2012.sav") # Glimpse both glimpse(cleaned_nilt) glimpse(unclean_nilt) ``` ::: The two data frames should *not* look the same. In `cleaned_nilt` the eight variables we coerced (`rsex`, `highqual`, `religcat`, `uninatid` and `ruhappy` as ``; `rage`, `rhourswk` and `persinc2` as ``) show their category labels or plain numbers, whereas in `unclean_nilt` every variable is still ``. If they look identical, the coerced version was not saved. ## Lab 4. Visual exploratory analysis {.unnumbered} Preamble code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Load the packages library(tidyverse) # Load the data from the .rds file we created in the last lab nilt <- readRDS("data/nilt_r_object.rds") # Create subset nilt_subset <- nilt |> select(rsex, rage, highqual, religcat, uninatid, ruhappy, rhourswk, persinc2) ``` ::: ### Activity Using the `nilt_subset` object, complete the tasks below in the 'Lab-6-Visual.Rmd' file, which you created earlier. Insert a new chunk for each of these activities and include brief comments as text in the Rmd document to introduce the plots and discuss the results (tip ---leave an empty line between your text and the next chunk to separate the description and the plots): - Create a first-level header to start a section called "Categorical analysis"; ```markdown # Categorical analysis ``` - Create a simple bar plot using the `geom_bar()` geometry to visualize the political affiliation reported by the respondents using the variable `uninatid`; ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(nilt_subset, aes(x = uninatid)) + geom_bar() + labs(title = "Political affiliation", x = "Party") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Answers_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: - Based on the plot above, create a 'stacked bar plot' to visualize the political affiliation by religion, using the `uninatid` and `religcat` variables; ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(nilt_subset, aes(x = uninatid, fill = religcat)) + geom_bar() + labs( title = "Political affiliation by religion", x = "Party", fill = "Religion" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Answers_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: - Create a new first-level header to start a section called "Numeric analysis"; ```markdown # Numeric analysis ``` - Create a scatter plot about the relationship between personal income `persinc2` on the Y axis and number of hours worked a week `rhourswk` on the X axis; ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(nilt_subset, aes(x = rhourswk, y = persinc2)) + geom_point() + labs( title = "Income and number of hours worked a week", x = "Number of hours worked a week", y = "Personal income (£ a year)" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Answers_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: - Finally, create a box plot to visualize personal income `persinc2` on the Y axis and self-reported level of happiness `ruhappy` on the x axis... Interesting result, Isn't it? Talk to your neighbour or tutor about your results; ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(nilt_subset, aes(x = ruhappy, y = persinc2)) + geom_boxplot() + labs( title = "Personal income and happiness", x = "Happiness level", y = "Personal income (£ a year)" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Answers_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: - Briefly comment each of the plots as text in your Rmd file; - Knit the .Rmd document as HTML. The knitted file will be saved automatically in your project. You can come back to the Rmd file to make changes if needed and knit it again as many times as you wish. ## Lab 7. Correlation {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Load the packages library(tidyverse) library(haven) # Load the data from the .rds file we created in lab 3 nilt <- readRDS("data/nilt_r_object.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Age of respondent’s spouse/partner nilt$spage <- as.numeric(nilt$spage) # Migration nilt <- mutate_at(nilt, vars(mil10yrs, miecono, micultur), as.numeric) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # overall perception towards migrants nilt <- rowwise(nilt) |> # sum values mutate(mig_per = sum(mil10yrs, miecono, micultur, na.rm = T)) |> ungroup() |> # assign NA to values that sum 0 mutate(mig_per = na_if(mig_per, 0)) ``` ::: ### Activity 1 Using the `nilt` data object, visualize the relationship of the following variables by creating a new chunk. Run the chunk individually and comment on what you observe from the result as text in the Rmd file (remember to leave an empty line between your text and the chunk). - Create a scatter plot to visualize the correlation between the respondent's overall opinion in relation to migration `mig_per` and the respondent's age `rage`. Remember that we just created the `mig_per` variable by summing three variables which were in a 0-10 scale (the higher the value, the better the person's perception is). In `aes()`, specify `rage` on the X axis and `mig_per` on the Y axis. Use the `ggplot()` function and `geom_point()`. Also, include a straight line describing the points using the `geom_smooth()` function. Within this function, set the `method` argument to `'lm'`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nilt |> ggplot(aes(x = rage, y = mig_per)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") + labs( title = "Perception of migration vs age", x = "Respondent age", y = "Perception of migration (0-30)" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Answers_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: - What type of relationship do you observe? Comment the overall result of the plot and whether this is in line with your previous expectation. ### Activity 2 - Create a boxplot to visualize the relationship between the respondent's overall opinion in relation to migration `mig_per` (Y axis) and constitutional view `uninatid` (X axis). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nilt |> ggplot(aes(x = uninatid, y = mig_per)) + geom_boxplot() + labs( title = "Perception of migration by constitutional view", x = "Constitutional view", y = "Perception of migration (0-30)" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Answers_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: - Do you think the opinion towards migration differs among the groups? Re: The boxes overlap considerably, but unionist respondents have a slightly lower median (15) than nationalist respondents and those identifying with neither (17 for both). So there is a modest difference in the overall perception of migration between the groups, with a lot of variation within each group. ### Activity 3 - Compute a correlation matrix for `rage`, `persinc2`, `mil10yrs`, `miecono` and `micultur`, using `'pairwise.complete.obs'` and rounding to 3 decimals. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nilt |> select(rage, persinc2, mil10yrs, miecono, micultur) |> cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rage persinc2 mil10yrs miecono micultur rage 1.000 -0.036 -0.024 -0.029 -0.099 persinc2 -0.036 1.000 0.165 0.199 0.195 mil10yrs -0.024 0.165 1.000 0.716 0.627 miecono -0.029 0.199 0.716 1.000 0.665 micultur -0.099 0.195 0.627 0.665 1.000 ``` ::: ::: - Is personal income or age correlated with the perception of migrants? Re: Age is not correlated with any of the three migration variables (all coefficients are close to 0, between -0.02 and -0.10). Personal income shows a weak positive correlation with all three (around 0.17 to 0.20): respondents with higher incomes tend to report slightly more positive views of the effects of migration on the economy (`miecono`), on culture (`micultur`) and on Northern Ireland over the last ten years (`mil10yrs`). The three migration variables are strongly correlated with each other (0.63 to 0.72), which is why combining them into `mig_per` is reasonable. ## Lab 8. Linear model. Simple linear regression {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Load the packages library(tidyverse) # Read the data from the .rds file nilt <- readRDS("data/nilt_r_object.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m3 <- lm(persinc2 ~ rhourswk, data = nilt) ``` ::: ### Lab activities Use the `nilt` data set object in your 'Lab-8-Simple-Linear-Regression.Rmd' file to: 1. Plot a scatter plot using `ggplot`. In the aesthetics, locate `rhourswk` in the X axis, and `persinc2` in the Y axis. In the `geom_point()`, jitter the points by specifying the `position = 'jitter'`. Also, include the best fit line using the `geom_smooth()` function, and specify the `method = 'lm'` inside. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(nilt, aes(x = rhourswk, y = persinc2)) + geom_point(position = "jitter") + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Answers_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: 2. Print the summary of `m3` using the `summary()` function. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(m3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = persinc2 ~ rhourswk, data = nilt) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -43694 -8148 -3070 4990 58249 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 5170.4 1966.2 2.63 0.00884 ** rhourswk 463.2 52.4 8.84 < 2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 13860 on 455 degrees of freedom (747 observations deleted due to missingness) Multiple R-squared: 0.1466, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1447 F-statistic: 78.15 on 1 and 455 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: 3. Is the relationship of hours worked a week significant? Re: Yes. The p-value (fourth column of the 'Coefficients' table) is lower than 0.05. 4. What is the adjusted r-squared? How would you interpret it? Re: the adjusted R-squared is 0.14. This can be interpreted in terms of percentage, e.g. 14% of the variance in personal income can be explained by the number of hours worked a week. 5. What is the sample size to fit the model? Re: The total number of observations in the data set is 1,204 and the model summary says that 747 observations were deleted due to missingness. Therefore, the sample size is 457 (1204-747). 6. What is the expected income in pounds a year for a respondent who works 30 hours a week according to coefficients of this model? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 5170.4 + 463.2 * 30 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 19066.4 ``` ::: ::: 7. Plot a histogram of the residuals of `m3` using the `residuals()` function inside `hist()`. Do the residuals look normally distributed (as in a bell-shaped curve)? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hist(residuals(m3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Answers_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Overall, the residuals look normally distributed with the exception of the values to the right-hand side of the plot (between 40000 and 60000). ## Lab 9. Multiple linear regression (part 1) {.unnumbered} ### Lab activities Load the packages and the data that you will need in your file using the code below: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Load the packages library(moderndive) library(tidyverse) # Read the data from the .rds file nilt <- readRDS("data/nilt_r_object.rds") ``` ::: 1. Print a table for the highest level of qualification `highqual` using the `table()` function. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} table(nilt$highqual) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Degree level or higher Higher education GCE A level or equiv 230 102 243 GCSE A-C or equiv GCSE D-G or equiv No qualifications 185 82 281 Other, level unknown Unclassified 27 54 ``` ::: ::: 2. Generate a scatter plot using `ggplot`. Within `aes()`, locate the number of hours worked a week `rhourswk` on the X axis and the personal income `persinc2` on the Y axis, and specify the `color` of the dots by the highest level of qualification `highqual`. Use the `geom_point()` function and 'jitter' the points using the argument `position`. Add the parallel slopes using the `geom_parallel_slopes()` function and set the standard error `se` to `FALSE`. What is your interpretation of the plot? Write down your comments to introduce the plot. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(nilt, aes(x = rhourswk, y = persinc2, color = highqual)) + geom_point(position = "jitter") + moderndive::geom_parallel_slopes(se = FALSE) + labs( title = "Personal income", subtitle = "Personal income and number of hours worked a week by education level", x = "Number of hours worked a week", y = "Personal income (£ a year)", color = "Highest education level" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Answers_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: 3. Fit a linear model using the `lm()` function to analyse the personal income `persinc2` using the number of hours worked a week `rhourswk`, the highest level of qualification `highqual`, and the age of the respondent `rage` as independent variables. Store the model in an object called `m4` and print the summary. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m4 <- lm(persinc2 ~ rhourswk + rage + highqual, nilt) summary(m4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = persinc2 ~ rhourswk + rage + highqual, data = nilt) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -36228 -6425 -1411 4635 54749 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 3904.64 2714.25 1.439 0.151 rhourswk 444.79 45.32 9.814 < 2e-16 *** rage 236.59 48.47 4.881 1.47e-06 *** highqualHigher education -8164.91 1939.50 -4.210 3.09e-05 *** highqualGCE A level or equiv -12439.26 1563.42 -7.956 1.47e-14 *** highqualGCSE A-C or equiv -13037.47 1703.07 -7.655 1.20e-13 *** highqualGCSE D-G or equiv -11622.07 2665.38 -4.360 1.61e-05 *** highqualNo qualifications -12968.10 2339.78 -5.542 5.11e-08 *** highqualOther, level unknown 15445.70 3334.75 4.632 4.76e-06 *** highqualUnclassified -12399.58 2786.16 -4.450 1.08e-05 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 11830 on 447 degrees of freedom (747 observations deleted due to missingness) Multiple R-squared: 0.3887, Adjusted R-squared: 0.3764 F-statistic: 31.58 on 9 and 447 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: 4. Comment on the results of the model by mentioning which of the variables is significant and their respective p-value, the adjusted r-squared of the model, and the number of observations used to fit the model. Re: All the independent variables including the number of hours worked a week, age, and all the categories of highest qualification level compared to 'Degree level or higher' are significant to predict personal income in the model 'm4', considering that the p-value is lower than 0.05. We can confirm this from the fourth column of the 'Coefficients' table. The adjusted R-squared of the model is 0.38 (0.3764 in the output). This means that 37.6% of the variance in personal income can be explained by these variables. The size of the sample used to fit this model is 457, considering that the 'nilt' data set contains 1204 observations but 747 were deleted due to missingness (1204 - 747). ## Lab 10. Multiple linear regression (part 2) {.unnumbered} Returning to the model `m4` from the Lab 9 activities: 1. Comment on the R2, adjusted R2, and F-statistic to interpret the model fit. Re: The R2 is 0.389 and the adjusted R2 is 0.376, so the number of hours worked, age and highest qualification together explain around 38% of the variation in personal income among the respondents in the model. The F-statistic is 31.6 on 9 and 447 degrees of freedom with a p-value far below 0.05, so the model as a whole is statistically significant - the independent variables explain more variation than would be expected by chance. 2. How many observations were removed due to missing values? Which variables are contributing to this? Re: 747 observations were deleted due to missingness, leaving 457 of the 1,204 respondents. We can check where the missing values come from by counting the NAs in each variable: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nilt |> select(persinc2, rhourswk, rage, highqual) |> summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` persinc2 rhourswk rage highqual Min. : 260 Min. : 4.00 Min. :18.00 No qualifications :281 1st Qu.: 6760 1st Qu.: 25.25 1st Qu.:35.00 GCE A level or equiv :243 Median :11960 Median : 37.00 Median :48.00 Degree level or higher:230 Mean :16395 Mean : 35.09 Mean :49.62 GCSE A-C or equiv :185 3rd Qu.:22100 3rd Qu.: 40.00 3rd Qu.:64.00 Higher education :102 Max. :75000 Max. :100.00 Max. :97.00 GCSE D-G or equiv : 82 NAs :307 NAs :638 NAs :3 (Other) : 81 ``` ::: ::: Most of the missing values come from `rhourswk` (638 NAs, as the question was only asked of respondents in work) and `persinc2` (307 NAs), with only 3 missing ages and no missing qualifications. As discussed in Lab 10, this means the model only describes respondents who are in work and reported their income, which needs to be borne in mind when interpreting the results. 3. Plot a histogram of the residuals for model `m4`. Do they look normally distributed? Can we trust our estimates or would you advise to carry out further actions to verify the adequate interpretation of this model? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hist(residuals(m4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Answers_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The distribution of the residuals in 'm4' looks overall normally distributed. However, the distribution is not perfectly symmetric. Therefore, we would advise conducting further checks to test the linear model assumptions.
